blogs.title: When “Similar Services” Means the Same Thing: The Court’s Take on DuPont Factor Two
blogs.description: This post dissects the Federal Circuit’s affirmation of the Board’s finding that credit‑card services and banking/financing services are “highly similar.” It explores the doctrinal history of the second DuPont factor, the impact of the Trademark ID Manual deletion, and how courts balance textual definitions versus functional realities in likelihood‑of‑confusion analyses. The article also considers the broader implications for new entrants into overlapping financial service markets.

blogs.title: The Sixth DuPont Factor Re‑examined: Why Scope Matters in Third‑Party Mark Surveys
blogs.description: An in‑depth look at the court’s vacatur of the Board’s narrow application of factor six. The blog explains the requirement to consider all similar marks on similar goods, evaluates the error of limiting the analysis to “credit‑card” marks, and discusses how this decision may reshape evidence‑gathering strategies for trademark oppositions, especially in crowded financial‑services sectors.

blogs.title: First Factor Fallout: How Commercial Strength and Impression Pivot on the Sixth Factor
blogs.description: This entry analyzes why the Federal Circuit tied the first factor’s commercial‑impression analysis to the sixth factor’s finding of mark strength. It reviews the interplay between mark distinctiveness, evidentiary burden, and the court’s reasoning that a remand on factor six necessitates a fresh look at factor one, offering guidance for practitioners on presenting strength/weakness evidence.

blogs.title: Procedural Lessons from Apex Bank v. CC Serve: De Novo Review, Substantial Evidence, and the Limits of Board Discretion
blogs.description: A procedural‑focused commentary on the appellate standards applied in the case—de novo review of legal conclusions and substantial‑evidence review of factual findings. The post highlights how the court parsed the Board’s discretion, the significance of vacatur versus affirmation, and what trademark practitioners can learn about crafting arguments that survive both factual and legal scrutiny on appeal.
